author: Hermann Hesse
introFa: کتاب «The Glass Bead Game» نوشته Hermann Hesse یکی از منابع ارزشمند و معتبر برای یادگیری زبان انگلیسی در سطح C2 است. این اثر با ساختاری منسجم و غنی، شما را در تسلط بر واژگان و درک مطلب یاری می‌کند.
readingTipsFa: پیش از مطالعه هر بخش از کتاب «The Glass Bead Game»، نگاهی سریع به تیترها و ساختار آن بیندازید.
واژگان و اصطلاحات جدید را در زمینه و بافت جمله یادداشت کنید تا در حافظه بلندمدت تثبیت شوند.
پس از پایان هر فصل، نکات کلیدی و آموخته‌های خود را مرور کرده و به زبان خود خلاصه کنید.

content: – 47 – The Glass Bead Game: Archaeometric evidence for the existence of an Etruscan glass industry by Andy Towle and Julian Henderson A B S T R A C T G lass historians have long posited the existence of an Etruscan glass industry on the basis of artefact forms distributed within the Etruscan koine. Principally this has been the core-formed glass vessels known as stachelflaschen, whose distinc- tive decoration is unique to Etruscan contexts. Given an apparent independent European Bronze Age glass industry, with the most comprehensive archaeological evidence for it in Northern Italy, the possibility of an independent Etruscan industry also seems possible. The first chemical analyses of several stachelflaschen, a leech-shaped brooch slider and some, less diagnostic, Etruscan glass beads from British collections are discussed here. The tech- nology embedded in the chemistry of these artefacts suggests that a diagnostic Etruscan glass technology was used to make beads rather than the ornate vessels. Reference is made to the compositional results of glass from the cemetery of Magdaleska Gora in Slovenia. I N T R O D U C T I O N As part of a broader study of ancient glass from Italian contexts from ca. 1200 – ca. 200 BC,1 eighteen samples of “Etruscan” glass were chemically characterised using electron microprobe analysis. The samples were all taken from objects held in museum collections.2 Despite the poor provenance of a number of the artefacts, the forms include core-formed vessels and brooch decoration previously attributed to Etruscan manufacture, along with less diagnostic beads. Previous arguments for the possible existence of an Etruscan glass industry have been strengthened by the demonstration of an earlier glass industry in Northern Italy (and elsewhere), using a distinct glassmaking technology (mixed alkali glass and glassy faience) defined by the analysis of material from the Final Bronze Age sites of Frattesina, Mariconda and Montagnana3 and middle bronze age and later (compositionally related) glassy faience and faience from Grotte Vittorio Vecchi and Vicofertile,4 Frabulino, Chiaromonte,5 and Poviglio.6 Given the sophisticated pyrotechnology of the Etruscan metal and ceramic Brought to you by | University of Georgia Libraries Authenticated Download Date | 6/7/15 7:02 AM

– 48 – industries, it is likely that glassmaking lay within the technical capability of the Etruscans. This study was an attempt to characterise Etruscan material and relate it to the earlier glass- making technology and contemporary production in the Mediterranean. T H E A R T E F A C T S The stachelflaschen. The earliest core-formed glass vessels found in Italy are certainly exotic imports: cups recov- ered from Etruscan contexts dated to the last quarter of the 8th century BC and probably hav- ing a Phoenician or Assyrian origin.7 However, there is a series of vessels which appear to be a class of artefact limited to Etruscan contexts from c. 650-550 BC: the stachelflaschen. This cat- egory of artefact was first defined by Haevernick in 1959, who recognised these core-formed glass vessels as a uniquely Etruscan phenomenon.8 The vessels were produced using the con- ventional core-formed technique of applying hot glass to a friable core on a rod, which was ––––––––––––––––––-––––– E x i s t e n c e o f a n E t r u s c a n G l a s s I n d u s t r y –-–––––––––––––––––––––– Figure 1 – Etruscan core-formed glass vessel, from which samples 11 and 12 were taken. – 49 – subsequently removed after the finished vessel had been annealed and cooled.9 The decora- tion is what distinguishes these vessels from contemporary products from Egypt, Rhodes and Mesopotamia. The vessels have a raised scale decoration, consisting of either applied knops of glass, or drawn from the body of the object (see Figure 1. Depending upon the underlying vessel form, a foot, base, neck, col- lar and handle may be added. Although a number of different coloured glasses have been used to make this form (amber, green and blue) all are monochrome (and mostly blue, either turquoise or dark blue opaque coloured). The decoration has been compared with that on a series of brooch decorations, which are contemporary, but are distributed outside the Etruscan zone from Este in Northern Italy to Yugoslavia and Slovenia.10 Since Haevernick’s initial study iden- tifying the type and listing twelve known examples, additional work by other authors have extended the number to over 100.11 Seventy two have a known provenance.12 The most common form is the oinochoe (see figure 1 above), but examples are also known in the forms of alabastron, pyx, lagynos and arybal- los. These forms can be related to Greek and Eastern Mediterranean models in ceramic and metal, but given the widespread adoption of these shapes around the Mediterranean, the forms themselves do not indicate origin, although the slightly elongated oinochoe form has parallels in Etruscan-produced ceramics.13 Haevernick initially suggested a 4th century BC date on the basis on general form, which was soon amended, to the late 7th century BC in the face of contextual data.14 Harden (1981, 139) argues for a long chronology for these vessels on the basis of art-historical discussion of the underlying form, and suggests a period from the late 7th century to the early 3rd century BC. Giuntoli, however rejects this, and after close examination of the few well- provenienced examples suggests a date of 650-550 for the entire group on the basis of archaeological context.15 The decoration on the vessels may have ––––––––––––––––––––––––––––– A n d y T o w l e a n d J u l i a n H e n d e r s o n ––––––––––––––––––––––––––––– figure 2 – Leech-Shaped brooch decoration from Rebato, held by Este Museum. Scale 1:1 figure 3 – Etruscan earring with beads from which samples 150-152 were taken. The unla- belled bead is made of amber. – 50 – parallels with early 7th century BC Etruscan ceramic vases.16 As yet there is no direct evidence for glass work- ing or making from Etruscan contexts.17 Nevertheless, these vessels have been assumed to have been manufactured with- in the Etruscan koine on the basis of their distinct decora- tion and limited distribution. On this basis, there is a suggestion that glass working rather than glass-making may have occurred. Many of the known examples are of unknown provenance, and are scattered amongst collections around the world. Leech-shaped brooch decoration. A series of brooch decorations made from glass have been noted as peculiar to Early Iron Age and Etruscan contexts in Central and Northern Italy.18 Their full distribution however, extends from Central Italy northwards as far as Poland, but is concentrated around the Northern Adriatic,19 including the cemetery of Magdalenska Gora in Slovenia.20These dec- orations take the form of a leech-shaped agglomeration of glass formed into the bow of the brooch on a rod, which has then been decorated with the addition of trails of differently coloured glass wrapped around the glass matrix. The trails of glass are marvered flush with the surface of the main body of the brooch before being combed in alternate directions to create a feathered or chevron design. Often the combing action leaves a ribbed finish in the glass, which has not been removed by further marvering. The colours used include blue, yel- low, white and red opaque glasses, although they may often be difficult to discern because of surface degradation. Whilst the chevron design is a common decorative motif in glass ves- sels from the Eastern Mediterranean region from the 14th century BC onwards,21 its use on brooch decoration (sometimes referred to as brooch sliders) is more restricted. Beads with a similar decoration have been noted from Northern Italy to Greece,22 and whilst these may originate in the same production as the brooch sliders, they may simply represent the noted widespread adoption of this decorative form. Rod-formed bracelets of similar design have also been recovered from Central and Northern Italy.23 There has been no previous attempt to chemically characterise the glasses employed to make these artefacts. It has been assumed that they were produced in Central and Northern Italy on the basis of their distribution. Beads. The Etruscan beads analysed in this study are all from the Beck Collection held by Cambridge University Museum. All are unexceptional in form or colour: either annular or globular beads ––––––––––––––––––-––––– E x i s t e n c e o f a n E t r u s c a n G l a s s I n d u s t r y –-–––––––––––––––––––––– figure 4 – SEM images and EDS spectra for Etruscan potash glasses 159 and 160. – 51 – T H E E T R U S C A N M A T E R I A L A N D S C I E N T I F I C A N A L Y S I S The group of samples defined here as Etruscan are from artefacts of diverse provenance, some of which have been assigned an Etruscan origin on grounds of typology rather than secure archaeological context. Nonetheless, this collection of samples represents a diverse range of artefacts and permits useful observations on the relationship between Etruscan glasses and the Final Bronze Age mixed-alkali glassmaking tradition. Eighteen samples: 10, 11, 12, 150 - 161, 176 - 178 inclusive. The Etruscan samples are all taken from material held in the UK, since approaches to Italian institutions for samples of Etruscan glass were unsuccessful. They are from several museum collections: Lincoln County Museum, National Museums and Galleries on Merseyside, Bristol City Museum and from Cambridge University Museum of Archaeology. The artefacts ranged from core-formed glass vessels to beads and complex brooch decorations, variously dated to the period 800-500 BC. In addition samples of glass artefacts from the Magdalenska Gora cemetery housed in the Peabody Museum Harvard College have been analysized. Samples were removed by pressure flaking small chips of glass of about 1mm from each artefact and mounting in epoxy resin blocks. The samples were polished flat with decreasing grades of grinding pastes down to 1 micron. The blocks were carbon coated to make the surface conductive to electrons and each sample was analysed using a Cambridge Microscan 9 electron microprobe. The samples were analysed using an 80 micron diameter defocused electron beam with an accelerating voltage of 20kV and a probe current of 40nA. The operating conditions, accuracy and precision are discussed in detail elsewhere.24 The results for twenty-two oxides were collected. An R.J. Lee Scanning Electron Microscope with ED analysis specifically designed to detect light ele- ments was also used so as to image and separately analyse any crystallites present. The glass types Three distinct types of glass have been detected: (1) High potassium glass (5 examples: 150, 151, 159, 160 and 161) (2) high magnesia (plant ash) soda-lime-silica glass (1 example: sample 152) and (3) low magnesia (natron) soda-lime-silica glass (12 examples: 10, 11, 12, 153, 154, 155, 156, 157, 158, 159, 176, 177, 178). Clearly these glass types cannot be considered as coming from a single glassmaking tradition. The variable provenance means that it is useful to discuss these glasses initially in terms of their general compositional type, before consideration of form and association. The high potassium glasses are a remarkable phenomenon: they are all very similar in composition, and no soda has been detected in them. They are all undecorated blue translucent annular beads. More specifically, these glasses are characterised by their high potassium oxide content (mean 16.29 %, range 14.73 - 17.70 %), and an absence of soda (i.e. below the lower ––––––––––––––––––––––––––––– A n d y T o w l e a n d J u l i a n H e n d e r s o n ––––––––––––––––––––––––––––– Brought to you by | University of Georgia Libraries Authenticated Download Date | 6/7/15 7:02 AM

– 52 – limit of detection for the machine used here: 0.01 % Na2O).25 The lack of soda is most unusu- al, and without parallel in the glass literature for all ancient periods of production. However, there is no reason to doubt the quality of the analyses. They have no overall lack of alkali, which might indicate a depletion of alkali as a result of weathering. Moreover, all totals approach 100 % and the samples were not analysed consecutively, showing that a temporary machine error is not responsible for the low soda values. – 53 – the detection of low atomic weight elements. Spectra from these analyses have no charac- teristic sodium peak (Figure 4). Several aspects of the glass chemistry could suggest the use of a terrestrial plant ash as the alkali source and others the use of a mineral source. The high potassium oxide lev- els are accompanied by extremely high phosphorus pentoxide and rather high cal- cium oxide levels. The phos- phorous pentoxide results have a mean value of 6.19%, and a range of 5.44% - 7.34% com- pared to a mean of 0.12 % and a range of 0 - 0.5 % for the other main “Etruscan” group of natron (LMG) glasses, and a mean of 11.47 % calcium oxide with a range of 10.6%- 12.51 % compared with a mean value of 6.62 %, and a range of 3.25% - 8.56% for the other glasses. However, the magnesia levels remain remarkably low for a glass made with a plant ash: a mean value 0.31% and a range of 0.24% - 0.38 %. So although the high potassium and phosphorus values could suggest that wood ash was used to make the glasses,26 the low magnesia levels would suggest a mineralogical source was used. If we were to suggest that some kind of purification of the wood ashes had taken place it is difficult to reconcile the fact that magnesia would have been reduced, but not (apparently) calcium oxide. Therefore a mineral potassium source perhaps associated with a low magnesia impurity seems a more like- ly alkali source. Had wood ash been used as an alkali source calcium would have been associat- ed with it. Since we are suggesting that this is not the case a separate calcium source would have been used, perhaps also in mineral form. Such a mineral is hydroxyapatite, the main calcium- bearing mineral found in bone.27 Although five samples is a rather small number, a positive cor- relation (R2) value of +0.9628 for a plot of their calcium versus phosphorus pentoxide contents shows that indeed bone ash must have been the source of calcium used to make the glasses. These glasses are also characterised by their low alumina and iron oxide levels, reflecting a relatively pure silica source. They have mean values of 0.49% and 0.24% compared with generally higher levels detected in natron glasses. (Figure 5) The high potassium glasses are all blue translucent and of a similar form. Samples 159, 160 and 161 are coloured with the use of cobalt oxide, containing 0.08, 0.05 and 0.06 % CoO respectively. Sample 150 contains no detectable cobalt oxide, and very low cop- per content (0.05 %): it is probably coloured by reduced iron oxide (0.24 %). Sample 151 contained very low cobalt oxide levels (0.02 %), which must be responsible for the glass’s colour, in the absence of any copper. ––––––––––––––––––––––––––––– A n d y T o w l e a n d J u l i a n H e n d e r s o n ––––––––––––––––––––––––––––– figure 5 – Correlation between calcium oxide and phosphorus pentoxide Brought to you by | University of Georgia Libraries Authenticated Download Date | 6/7/15 7:02 AM

– 55 – es (a range of 5.44% to 7.34 %), is not matched in the Frattesina glasses (0.14 - 0.25 %). The two groups are also markedly different in their lime levels, with much greater quantities found in the Etruscan group (10.6% - 12.51 % compared to 2.05% - 3.15 %). The Etruscan high potassium glasses are therefore quite distinct from the earlier Frattesina high potassium glasses, which can readily be regarded as a variant of the mixed-alkali technology. Four of the Etruscan high potassium glasses contain elevated arsenious oxide levels. This may be associated with the use of arsenic-rich cobalt for blue colorant, but there is no sim- ple correlation between these components, with sample 150 containing 0.85 % As2O5, but no detectable cobalt oxide. The two samples with the highest arsenic content also contain the great- est amount of copper oxide (samples 150 and 161), which may indicate the use of an arsenic- rich copper, though the copper levels can more readily be viewed as impurities. Arsenic can eas- ily boil off during the preparation of metal ores, which may account for the variation in the lev- els seen here: its presence remains significant, but at present not entirely explicable. Arsenic rich colorant materials were introduced in glass technology in the 17th century AD. Nonetheless, the appearance of the beads does not suggest that they were made at that time, but considerably earlier and the high phosphorus levels would be anomalous for glass of such a date.29 The Etruscan material is therefore a significant discovery. The technology involved would appear to employ a mineral potassium source combined with bone ash and relatively pure silica source, perhaps a quartz sand. The low magnesia levels are probably to be considered as impurities. Two of the high potassium glass beads are from a single artefact: threaded on a copper alloy “earring” (Figure 3),30 and are associated with a further anomalous composition: the only high magnesia plant ash glass in the “Etruscan” group (Table 5). Samples 159 - 161 are from an uncatalogued group from the Beck Collection labelled “Etruscan, 800 - 600 BC, from Florence.. The plant ash glass (sample 152), which was associ- ated with samples 150 and 151 contains 4.38 % magnesia and an elevated level of potassium oxide (2.33 %). Both of these composi- tional features are consistent with an ancient plant ash glass composition.31 All of the other glasses have low-magnesia compositions, consistent with the use of a natron type soda source (see Table 2). The natron group of glasses (n=10) are of variable provenance, but are united by their compositional type. The diversity of their origins is however reflected in the varia- tions in the alumina levels found and to the variation in potassium oxide levels which for some samples reaches the levels found in plant ash glasses (maximum 2.6%). The com- positional variation within the natron glass type is also illustrated by the composition range of calcium oxide levels (3.35%-8.56%). – 57 – Whilst three samples from two artefacts does not represent a comprehensive survey of Etruscan glass vessels, the results are worth commenting upon. Firstly it is interesting to note that despite their separate provenance, the two vessels have a similar chemical composition. The glasses used to make these Etruscan vessels were fabricated from natron and a sand rich in shell fragments. They have a low phosphorus pentoxide content (avg. = 0.02 wt.%), and raised chlorine and sulphur oxide levels associated with the use of a natron alkali source. The vessels can be distinguished compositionally by the colouring agents used: both contain copper (1.04 and 1.99 wt.% respectively). The darker, more densely coloured vessel also contains 0.11 wt.% cobalt oxide, sufficient to give the piece its hue. The chemical composition of the glass leech-shaped slider on an Etruscan broach is typ- ical of a natron glass (Table 5, 176-178). These analyses can be compared to the (unpub- lished) electron microprobe analyses of two of these brooch sliders from the cemetery of Magdaleska Gora, Slovenia.32 The natron glass compositions are entirely consistent with analyses 176-178. However it is notable that the translucent brown matrices and the dec- orations of the Magdalenska Gora examples and the yellow decoration of the slider (176) are characterised by low alumina levels of between 0.26% and 0.43%. Since this is found also in other Etruscan artefacts made from natron glass (Table 5) and is relatively unusu- al amongst the results for (especially later) natron glasses, in the long run it may turn out to be diagnostic of an Etruscan glass technology. Most importantly, these analyses demonstrate no link whatsoever between the North Italian mixed-alkali glassmaking tradition and the kind of glass that was used to make Etruscan core-formed glass vessels, natron glass. Colorants The colorants used for the high potassium glasses have been briefly discussed above. The “Etruscan” group of glasses includes 9 blue translucent glasses (samples 10, 11, 12, 150, 151, 158, 159, 160 and 161), 3 transparent colourless glasses (samples 153, 154 and 155), 2 white opaque glasses (samples 157 and 178), 2 red opaque glasses (samples 156 and 177), 1 yellow opaque (sample 176) and 1 green translucent glass (sample 152). The dominant colorant in the blue translucent glasses (samples 150 and 10) is copper oxide (0.05% and 1.05 % copper oxide respectively). Samples 151 and 158 must have been coloured with very low cobalt content (0.02 % in each), with no copper being detected and 0.12 % cupric oxide respectively. Samples 160, 161, 12, 159 and 11 were all definitely coloured with cobalt (with 0.05, 0.06, 0.08, 0.08 and 0.11 % CoO). The three colourless transparent glass samples were taken from a fragmentary brooch decoration and from two annular beads (samples 153 - 155). Intriguingly, all three contain CoO at levels of 0.05, 0.11 and 0.02 respectively. The first two cobalt levels might be expected to colour the glasses blue but in this case surprisingly it has not occurred, perhaps because the cobalt is present as a reduced ion. – 58 – Sample 157 is a white opaque glass decoration on a red opaque bead, coloured using tin oxide (2.37 % SnO2). The lead content of this glass (2.25 % PbO) sug- gests that the glass may originally have been intended to be coloured opaque yellow using lead stannate (PbSnO3). When heated above 900 °C, lead stannate decomposes to tin oxide, a process that is irreversible. The earliest use of tin oxide (and lead stannate) to colour and opacify glasses is dated to the 2nd century BC onwards.33 Given the relatively poor provenance, it seems most likely that this particular artefact has been misidentified as Etruscan,34 and was actually made later than the Etruscan era. The other “white” opaque glass (sample 178) is from the combed decoration of a leech - shaped brooch slider. Initially considered an accidental addition, possibly of quartz, upon analysis it proved to be a fragment of glass and must have been deliberate- ly attached to the brooch. Backscattered SEM imaging and EDS analysis demonstrated that an EMPA analysis of the sample was of glass adhering to the edge of a silica-rich core. Examination of the vitreous phase adhering to the silica-rich lump showed it to contain inclusions with very high copper contents, antimony and arsenic, suggesting that this was a glass coloured red with reduced copper oxide from an unusual scrap bronze (Figure 6). The two red opaque glasses (156 and 177) are from the same composite artefacts as the white opaque samples (i.e. a bead and a brooch slider). Sample 156 has a low cop- per oxide content of 0.19 %, and a raised iron oxide level of 7.34%. It was initially assumed that the colour was due to the copper being in the reduced cuprous state. Iron acting as a reducing agent has been noted as a method of facilitating the dissolution of copper oxide into a glass, and the subsequent precipitation of cuprite. Sample 177 has a similarly low copper oxide content (0.67 %) and raised iron level (3.88 %), and may be coloured in the same way. SEM imaging of the samples failed to identify copper rich inclusions- either cuprite or metallic copper in the glass matrix. Since both of these glass- es contain high iron levels, additional consideration was given to the possibility of iron oxides being used as a colorant in a reduced precipitated form. A number of authors have noted the use of iron oxide as a colorant of red enamels.35 In the examples discussed in previous studies, finely ground red iron oxide (haematite) and uncoloured glass were mixed and rapidly fused to another surface. Both high-lead and soda-lime-silica glasses have been employed, but in each case the process is regarded as having been rapid to avoid complete fusion and dissolution of the iron oxide into the glass matrix, and there- by losing its colouring properties (Verità 1998, 131-132). The capacity of either high-lead or soda-lime silica glass to be sufficiently hot to be workable and simultaneously contain undissolved red iron oxide has yet to be determined, and might usefully be established by experimental work. D I S C U S S I O N O F T H E R E S U L T S F O R “ E T R U S C A N ” G L A S S E S Although the sites of Cumae and Pozzouli are sometimes considered to be within the Etruscan cultural sphere, these cities are located South of the Etruscan heartland, and were both principally Greek settlements. For these reasons, and their distinct chemical composition, samples from these sites are considered separately.36 Given the poor provenance of several of the “Etruscan” items, and the likely inclu- sion of several later glasses (see above), a certain circumspection is required when discussing this collection of analyses. The principle observation to be made concerning the Etruscan glasses is that there is no evidence for continuity or shared technological tradition with the Final Bronze Age glass technology found in the Po valley. This is an important observation since it has been suggested that Frattesina may represent some form of early proto-Etruscan colony in the Po Valley.37 It can now be seen that the technological milieu of the Frattesina glass industry is more closely related to a longstanding and more widely distributed European tradition than that employed in the (later) Etruscan world. Despite the presence of distinct typological forms (such as the stachelflaschen), the chemical composition of the Etruscan glasses considered above is neither sufficiently homogenous nor distinct to be classified as a separate diagnostic technological tradition. Whilst there can be no doubt about the technological sophistication of Etruscan high temperature industries,38 there is as yet no direct evidence for glassmaking or glasswork- ing from Etruscan contexts: however the unique forms would suggest that glass working, at least, was taking place in secondary production centres presumably using imported raw glass, perhaps from Levantine production centres. Nevertheless, the presence of the high potassium glasses in this group suggests that a distinct technological tradition was present after all, and one might prove to be diagnostic of the Etruscan world. Unfortunately the forms and colour of the artefacts (blue translucent undecorated annular beads) can not be claimed as being sufficiently diagnostic when attempting to select similar samples for further analysis. There is a clear need for additional analyses of well provenanced glass objects from Etruscan contexts. – 60 – contemporary glass, tends to suggest that glass production was both highly localised and uncontrolled. Whilst it is not, at present, possible to locate individual manufacturing cen- tres, nor may it ever be so, it seems likely that production of glass found in Etruscan con- texts was produced in a non-centralised system without the compositional consistency which characterises so many other periods of glass production. Whereas from the Middle Bronze Age to Final Bronze Age (1600-900 BC) much of the glass consumed by com- munities in Central and Northern Italy (and elsewhere in Europe) tended to be compo- sitionally consistent, whether of mixed-alkali, high potassium or soda lime plant ash glasses, albeit with some evidence of regional production,39 some of the glasses deposit- ed during the Early Iron Age to the Roman Period (900-300 BC) are far more composi- tionally variable. The glasses from Cumae and Pozzouli are an exception to this and will be discussed elsewhere.40 C O N T I N U I T Y A N D T R A D I T I O N : I R O N A G E A N D E T R U S C A N G L A S S There is no evidence for continuity of glass production from the Final Bronze Age into the Iron Age, either within or without the Villanovan/Etruscan koine of Central and Northern Italy. Instead, the chemical composition of glasses from these contexts represent a more complex picture of production and consumption. Although there are three distinct com- positional types being used by the Etruscans (high potassium, natron and plant ash glass- es), the transition from plant ash to natron soda-lime glasses can be recognised within this data set, suggesting that a significant proportion of the glass originated in the Eastern Mediterranean region, where such a transition probably occurred. However, glasses from Este, along with material analysed from Magdalenska Gora can be distinguished from material from the Eastern Mediterranean. One distinctive characteristic would appear to be the low alumina levels detected in the Etruscan glasses, which are more typical of Bronze Age plant ash glasses and reflect the use of a relatively pure silica source. Amongst the glasses there are examples that do not conform to the convention- al classification of either high/low magnesia soda-lime glasses (plant ash and natron glass- es), with intermediate contents of soda, potassium oxide and magnesia. These samples are characterised by highly variable compositions which suggests that they represent a glass technology that does not employ consistent proportions and sources of raw materials or a homogenising process (Table 5). This is an indication that the glass technology was in a transitional phase. Given the limited distribution of some of the glass forms, it seems like- ly that the glass production was localised to Italy and the northern Adriatic. A group of high-iron glasses recovered from Greek settlements in Southern Central Italy may rep- resent a new, highly localised glass type used for forms found across a large area (from the Aegean to Central Europe). The absence of data on further examples from elsewhere makes this an intriguing proposition. When compared with other samples of Italian prehistoric glasses, the relative levels of phosphorous pentoxide and potassium oxide shows a clear distinction between high potassium, mixed-alkali and natron glasses. ––––––––––––––––––-––––– E x i s t e n c e o f a n E t r u s c a n G l a s s I n d u s t r y –-–––––––––––––––––––––– Brought to you by | University of Georgia Libraries Authenticated Download Date | 6/7/15 7:02 AM

– 62 – C O N C L U S I O N S The chemical analyses discussed here have demonstrated that the stachelflaschen were made using a low-magnesia natron glass, similar to contemporary material from the Eastern Mediterranean and unrelated to the earlier mixed alkali glasses. Their chemical compositions do not substantiate the hypothesis of a distinct glassmaking tradition for them as has been suggested. This means that while it is unlikely that natron glass was made in Etruscan Italy, the tradition employed is closely associated with that of the Eastern Mediterranean. Therefore the Etruscan vessels may have been made from imported glass. Moreover, the Etruscan assemblage was not homogenous, and the high- ly variable glass chemistry of the group suggests that glass manufacture may have been localized (and technically less well controlled than during the Final Bronze Age). A num- ber of the samples, from undiagnostic annular beads of translucent glass, were of an exceptional high potassium glass type, one of which is distinct from the mixed alkali or any other defined glass tradition (including the Medieval high potassium glasses). They are an exciting discovery and it is possible these glasses are indicators that an independ- ent Etruscan glass technology existed. There is increasing scientific evidence for inde- pendent glass production in the prehistoric Mediterranean.41 Thus, whilst it remains difficult to speak of an Etruscan glass industry in the absence of direct evidence (i.e. partially fused raw materials, furnaces, crucibles and ingots) we can define the nature of the glass consumed in Etruscan contexts as having been produced in a non-centralised way using highly variable raw materials (both their types and origins) and as a technology which is distinct from earlier and later traditions. The high potassium glass beads are an intriguing hint of a possible distinct Etruscan glass- making tradition, which could be substantiated with the analysis of well-provenanced material. Therefore, glassmaking and working may have taken place alongside the impor- tation of raw natron glass and finished exotic items from the Eastern Mediterranean. Further investigation of glass from Etruscan contexts, preferably from securely- dated recently excavated deposits, would help to clarify this picture of glassmaking in Iron Age and Etruscan Italy. Rather than single or even regionally specific traditions, it would appear that glass production had highly variable characteristics, lacking the strong conformity which marks other contemporary production of ceramics and metalwork.
